summary: This was a week where geopolitics, central banks and AI-infrastructure economics all moved in the same direction at once, and each fed the others. The Iran-US Gulf war widened from tanker skirmishes into two overlapping maritime chokepoint crises -- Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb -- while the Fed, ECB and BOJ all leaned hawkish in the same five days, driving core sovereign yields to multi-year or multi-decade highs even as equities repeatedly shrugged the shocks off by the close. A running AI-capex subplot split the market into clear winners (foundry, hardware, infrastructure capex) and losers (memory, software incumbents), a divide that sharpened rather than resolved as the week went on. By Sunday the mood was less "crisis" than "multiple unresolved fronts heading into a genuinely loaded week" -- Monday's Oman talks, Wednesday's FOMC and next Thursday's BOJ decision all sit on the other side of the weekend. The throughline a day-by-day reader might miss: volatility gauges and credit spreads stayed remarkably calm all week despite the barrage of stacked shocks, a complacency that every theme below is quietly leaning on.

themes.title: Gulf war widens into two chokepoints, and oil can't decide which story to price
themes.detail: What began the week as tanker strikes and a Jordan base hit (Mon/Tue) escalated by Friday into Houthi forces seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast -- Mocha, the Hanish islands and Perim -- opening a second, unaddressed chokepoint at Bab el-Mandeb alongside Hormuz, and by the weekend a drone strike had knocked out Saudi Arabia's main pipeline bypass route entirely. Brent swung from near $100 early week to a $109.97 high on the widening war, then back to $104 on the first concrete diplomacy (Monday's Oman meeting) -- except Bahrain's last-minute refusal to attend and Iran's own lowered expectations suggest that de-escalation trade may be getting ahead of itself. VLCC freight rates hitting an all-time high near $800,000/day is the clearest sign the physical market isn't waiting for a deal to be priced -- tonnage is already being rerouted around both straits at once.

themes.title: Fed, ECB and BOJ all lean hawkish in the same week, and yields break out together
themes.detail: The ECB delivered its second hike of the year (to 2.50%) on Thursday, BOJ watchers moved to near-unanimous consensus for a September 17-18 hike to 1.25%, and Fed-hike odds for Wednesday's FOMC whipsawed between roughly 48% and 90% across the week as hot CPI and PPI prints collided with a stagflationary UMich miss. The result showed up everywhere in rates: Bund yields hit a 17-year high (3.51%), gilts an 18-year high near 5.38%, and US 10-years sat on the cusp of 5% for two straight sessions -- a genuinely synchronized global tightening repricing rather than a single-country story. Wednesday's FOMC and next week's BOJ decision are now the events that either confirm or unwind this entire week's rates move.

themes.title: AI capex splits into clear winners and losers -- and the split is widening, not narrowing
themes.detail: Oracle's $90-95bn capex guidance mid-week ignited a hardware rally (HPE and Dell +11%, Super Micro +7%, later extended by Dell's RBC upgrade), and TSMC's 53.3% y/y sales jump confirmed foundry capacity remains structurally short. On the other side, DeepSeek's ultra-lean V4.1 Flash architecture -- which cuts memory requirements by roughly 75% -- hit Samsung and SK Hynix hard on Friday and again framed Sunday's retirement of V4-Pro as forcing the industry toward memory-light inference, even as US suppliers Micron and SanDisk held up far better. Layer in the software-incumbent selloff (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Intuit) earlier in the week on GPT-6 disruption fears, and the pattern is consistent: infrastructure and foundry keep winning, memory and application-layer software keep absorbing the downside of the same AI buildout.

themes.title: Markets keep shrugging off each individual shock -- credit and vol stayed unusually calm
themes.detail: Despite a war widening on two fronts, three hawkish central banks and multi-decade-high government bond yields, the VIX spent the week oscillating in a fairly narrow 15-18 band, closing Friday at 15.84 after an 11% one-day drop, and US equities snapped a four-session losing streak on Friday's relief rally. High-yield and investment-grade credit spreads stayed near multi-cycle tights the entire week even as Treasury yields surged toward 5%, a rates-vs-credit divergence flagged repeatedly across the daily briefings. That gap between headline stress and priced risk is itself the week's quiet tell -- it leaves markets more exposed than the calm surface suggests if Monday's Oman talks disappoint or Wednesday's FOMC surprises hawkish.
